composition: Nominal composition Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-9Cr (wt%). The melt was made from high-purity Fe (99.99%), Mn (99.9%), Al (99.9%), C (99.8%) and Cr (99.9%). ICP-measured composition of the 9Cr strip is Fe balance, Mn 27.7, Al 9.5, C 1.3 and Cr 9.3 wt% (nominal target Cr 9). Cr is the systematically varied alloying element across the series (0Cr–9Cr), added to suppress κ-carbide precipitation, promote δ-ferrite and, per the literature cited, to improve corrosion/oxidation resistance and intercrystalline cohesion; Mn and C act as austenite stabilizers and solution/precipitation strengtheners, while Al provides the density reduction.
conclusions: Within the near-rapidly solidified Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr strip series, Cr addition increases the δ-ferrite fraction but reduces κ-carbide precipitation in austenite; the 9Cr strip shows the largest ferrite contribution (19.6 vol%) and forms Cr₂₃C₆ carbides at austenite grain boundaries instead of κ-carbides, while containing a very high austenite dislocation density. Its as-cast yield strength (740 ± 8 MPa) exceeds that of the Cr-free strip because increased dislocation density and Cr₂₃C₆ formation outweigh the loss of κ-carbide strengthening, and its UTS (979 ± 22 MPa) and strain-hardening rate (2385 MPa) are the highest of the series, but its ductility is the lowest (20.3 ± 5 %), attributed to the increase in dislocation density and to grain-boundary Cr₂₃C₆ causing intergranular cracking. Compared with the sibling strips, this illustrates the trade-off in which Cr raises strength and strain-hardening rate at the expense of elongation, making the 9Cr strip the strongest but least ductile as-cast member; the CeCr-type grain-boundary carbide effect is also carried over to the annealed 9Cr condition.
mechanisms: Cr addition expands the solid solubility of Al and C in Fe–Mn–Al–C steel and lowers the driving force for κ-carbide formation, so increasing Cr progressively suppresses κ-carbide precipitation; at 9 wt% Cr no κ-carbide superlattice is detected in the austenite SADP.

At 9 wt% Cr, carbon instead binds into Cr₂₃C₆ carbides, which precipitate in granular/banded form (about 100 nm wide) at austenite grain boundaries; these coarsening grain-boundary carbides promote inter-granular cracking and are identified as the reason for the lowest ductility of the as-cast (and annealed) 9Cr strip.

Cr addition raises the dislocation density in the as-cast austenite: rapid cooling generates thermal stress in all strips, while the reduced fraction/size of nano-scale κ-carbides increases the ability to form dislocations; the higher strain-hardening rate of Cr-containing strips corroborates this higher dislocation formation ability.

The 9Cr strip has a slightly lower austenite dislocation density than the 6Cr strip because the 9 wt% Cr addition further improves C solid solubility and inhibits κ-carbide precipitation, while precipitation of Cr₂₃C₆ consumes carbon and reduces dislocation formation.

Cr promotes δ-ferrite formation, and the resulting larger δ-ferrite fraction creates more δ-ferrite/austenite phase-interface area that blocks dislocation propagation, contributing to the reduced plasticity of Cr-containing strips.

The non-monotonic yield strength of as-cast strips with Cr (724 → 617 MPa, then rising to 740 MPa for 9Cr) is the balance of two opposing effects: reduced nano-scale κ-carbide precipitation lowers strength, while increased dislocation density and Cr₂₃C₆ precipitation raise it, the latter dominating at 9 wt% Cr so that its yield strength exceeds that of the Cr-free strip.

Cr addition greatly enhances the steady-stage strain-hardening rate (1626, 2048, 2266 and 2385 MPa for 0Cr, 3Cr, 6Cr, 9Cr) because fewer κ-carbides obstruct dislocation glide and generate slip bands, i.e. reduction of the glide-plane-softening effect of nano-scale κ-carbides that otherwise lowers the strain-hardening rate of the Cr-free strip.

Despite the lowest κ-carbide content and smallest κ-carbide size among the strips, the as-cast 6Cr (and by extension Cr-containing) strips show low elongation because their high initial dislocation density interferes with slip-band formation, showing that initial dislocation density, not only slip-band formation ability, controls ductility.
microstructure: Two-phase austenite (γ) + δ-ferrite, with austenite as the major continuous matrix and δ-ferrite uniformly dispersed in it. The 9Cr strip has the largest ferrite fraction of the series, 19.6 vol%, and the strongest δ-related XRD reflections (δ(110) at 2θ = 44.1°); the austenite lattice constant is 3.55 Å. OM shows δ-ferrite as the densest population of block-like particles of the four strips, some linked/interconnected into irregular networks in the austenite matrix; ferrite morphology shifts from rod-like (0Cr) to block-like with increasing Cr. The austenite contains a very high dislocation density (slightly lower than in the 6Cr strip) and shows no κ-carbide superlattice in SADP. Instead, Cr₂₃C₆ carbides (cubic, lattice constant 1.054 nm) form at austenite grain boundaries in granular or banded shapes about 100 nm wide. In the ferrite, nano-scale DO3 ordered phase appears (superlattice reflections with hkl all odd or all even, zone [011]δ+[011]DO3); only a few dislocations are occasionally seen in the ferrite. Solidification followed the FA (ferrite-to-austenite) mode, L → L+δ → L+δ+γ → δ+γ, so δ-ferrite nucleated and grew first from the melt and is found at grain centres.
processing: An alloy ingot made from high-purity Fe/Mn/Al/C/Cr was reheated to melt by an induction coil, then the liquid metal was poured into a copper mold rotating at 600 r/min in Ar atmosphere, giving a calculated maximum cooling rate of about 5×10³ K/s (near-rapid solidification). The resulting strip was (60–80) mm × 60 mm × 2.5 mm. This as-cast state is the terminal condition of the object and received no post-solidification heat treatment; annealing at 550 °C for 5 h (vacuum electric resistance furnace) defines separate annealed samples of the same alloy, not this as-cast strip.
properties: Density 6.43 g/cm³ (SJ-600G water-displacement analyzer), the lowest of the strip series (6.49, 6.45, 6.46 g/cm³ for 0Cr, 3Cr, 6Cr). Room-temperature tensile properties (strain rate 1×10⁻³ s⁻¹, gauge 20 mm × 4 mm × 1 mm, MTS Criterion Model 44, 10 kN; average of 3 measurements): yield strength 740 ± 8 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 979 ± 22 MPa, total elongation 20.3 ± 5 %; average steady-stage strain-hardening rate 2385 MPa, the highest of the series. Engineering stress–strain curve rises to near 1000 MPa with a small load drop before fracture and terminates near 22–26 % strain. Relative to the Cr-free 0Cr as-cast strip, the 9Cr strip has higher YS (740 vs 724 MPa) and higher UTS (979 vs 924 MPa) but clearly the lowest total elongation (20.3 % vs 40.8 %). Characterization techniques applied: OM (Zeiss Axio imager A2m), TEM with SADP (JEM-2100F, 200 kV), XRD (D/Max-2200, Cu target, 40 kV/40 mA, 4°/min), ICP for composition and water-displacement density measurement.
summary: As-cast 9Cr strip is the 9 wt% Cr member of the as-cast Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr (x = 0, 3, 6, 9 wt%) austenitic low-density steel strip series produced by centrifugal casting under near-rapid solidification (copper mold, 600 r/min, Ar, ~5×10³ K/s) to a thickness of 2.5 mm, with no post-solidification heat treatment. The work examines how Cr addition modifies microstructure, carbide formation (κ-carbide suppression and Cr₂₃C₆ precipitation) and the resulting strength–ductility balance. The 9Cr strip attains the highest as-cast ultimate tensile strength (979 ± 22 MPa) and strain-hardening rate (2385 MPa) of the series but the lowest total elongation (20.3 ± 5 %).
unmapped: The 9Cr strip exhibits the strongest δ(110) XRD reflection beside γ(111) of the four as-cast strips, confirming that Cr addition favors ferrite; ferrite fraction across the series is 10.2, 11.4, 14.8 and 19.6 vol% for 0Cr, 3Cr, 6Cr and 9Cr.

The as-cast strips are reported to be almost free of casting defects owing to the high feeding capacity supported by the large centrifugal force, and any remaining defects are randomly distributed, so casting defects are ruled out as a cause of the reduced plasticity of Cr-containing strips.

The strengthened strips are intended for weight-reduced automotive applications; near-rapid solidification centrifugal casting is presented as a simple, near-net-shape route that avoids coarse carbides and composition segregation of high-Mn, high-Al, high-C austenitic low-density steels.
